summary:
EARTHSONA is an interactive educational web application that transforms real Earth science observations into music, helping children aged 6–8 understand how our planet changes. Developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026's “The Earth Information Jukebox” challenge, the project combines Earth observation visualisations with data-driven sonification, allowing users to hear patterns in environmental data rather than relying on visual information alone.
The experience features three interactive missions: Ocean Symphony, Forest Voices, and Earth's Pulse. Each mission explores different aspects of our planet, translating measurements such as sea surface temperature, vegetation indices, air temperature, and precipitation into musical elements. A friendly virtual guide, Luna, helps explain the science in accessible language, while the Earth Sound Lab allows users to experiment with environmental variables through interactive simulations.
By making complex scientific information more engaging and accessible, EARTHSONA aims to encourage curiosity about Earth science while offering an alternative way to experience and understand environmental data, including for blind and low-vision learners.
details:
3.1 What exactly does EARTHSONA do?

EARTHSONA transforms environmental and Earth observation data into an interactive musical experience. It allows users to explore how different parts of the Earth change over time through a combination of scientific visualisations, interactive graphs, and sound.

The application is organised into three main missions:

1. Ocean Symphony – Listening to Our Oceans

This mission explores changes in sea surface temperature. Users can observe ocean temperature patterns and hear how changes in temperature are translated into musical pitch and other sound characteristics.

The mission aims to help users understand that the ocean is constantly changing and that temperature variations can be observed and studied using Earth observation data.

2. Forest Voices – Listening to Our Forests

This mission explores vegetation health and greenness using satellite-derived vegetation indices, including the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI).

Changes in vegetation measurements influence the generated musical output. For example, higher vegetation index values can produce higher pitches, while lower values produce lower pitches.

The mission introduces users to the idea that satellites can help scientists monitor vegetation conditions over time.

3. Earth's Pulse – Listening to Our Atmosphere

This mission explores atmospheric and weather-related variables, including air temperature, precipitation, and solar radiation.

These variables are translated into different musical characteristics. For example, precipitation can influence rhythmic activity, while temperature can influence pitch and solar radiation can influence sound brightness.

Together, the three missions demonstrate how scientific measurements can be transformed into a different form of communication.

3.2 How does it work?

EARTHSONA combines Earth observation datasets, data processing, visualisation, and real-time sound generation.

The process follows four main stages:

Stage 1 – Data collection

The application retrieves environmental datasets from NASA resources and supplementary external data providers. These datasets contain measurements that describe different aspects of the Earth's oceans, vegetation, and atmosphere.

Stage 2 – Data processing

The collected measurements are organised and processed so that they can be interpreted by the application. Relevant variables are normalised and mapped to defined sound parameters.

Stage 3 – Data-driven sonification

The application translates scientific measurements into musical characteristics.

Examples include:

  • Sea surface temperature influencing musical pitch.
  • Vegetation indices influencing pitch and harmonic richness.
  • Precipitation influencing rhythmic density.
  • Air temperature influencing pitch.
  • Solar radiation influencing sound brightness.

The sound is generated according to the underlying data and defined mapping rules. It is not simply background music played over environmental videos.

Stage 4 – Interactive exploration

Users can explore the visualisations, listen to the generated sounds, follow changes through time, and experiment with different environmental conditions in the Earth Sound Lab.

A virtual guide named Luna provides explanations and helps users understand the scientific concepts behind each mission.

3.3 What are the benefits of EARTHSONA?

Making Earth science more engaging

Environmental datasets can be difficult to understand, particularly for younger audiences. EARTHSONA presents scientific information through an interactive combination of visuals and sound.

Promoting accessibility

Sonification provides an additional way to communicate scientific information beyond visual representations. This can benefit blind and low-vision learners when supported by appropriate audio descriptions, keyboard navigation, screen-reader-compatible controls, and text equivalents.

Encouraging scientific curiosity

The three missions introduce users to oceans, vegetation, and atmospheric conditions, encouraging them to explore how scientists observe and study our planet.

Connecting data with human perception

By converting numerical measurements into musical patterns, EARTHSONA helps users experience changes in environmental data in a more intuitive and memorable way.

Supporting interactive learning

The Earth Sound Lab encourages experimentation by allowing users to adjust environmental variables and explore how different conditions can affect the generated sound. Simulated scenarios are distinguished from actual scientific observations.

3.4 What do we hope to achieve?

Our goal is to make Earth observation information more accessible, engaging, and understandable, particularly for younger learners.

We hope EARTHSONA demonstrates that scientific data does not have to be communicated exclusively through graphs, maps, and numerical values. Sound can provide another meaningful dimension through which people can explore environmental changes.

Ultimately, we want to encourage curiosity about our planet, introduce younger audiences to Earth observation science, and demonstrate the educational potential of data sonification.

3.5 Technologies, programming languages, tools, and software

Programming languages

  • TypeScript
  • JavaScript
  • Python

Frontend and visualisation

  • Vite
  • Three.js
  • Web-based interactive visualisations
  • Web Audio API / browser-based audio generation

Backend

  • Python
  • FastAPI

Artificial intelligence and voice

  • Google Gemini API for Luna's AI-powered conversational functionality.
  • Kokoro-82M text-to-speech for Luna's spoken responses.

Data and scientific resources

  • Microsoft Planetary Computer
  • Meteomatics Weather API
  • NASA Earth observation datasets and visualisations
  • NOAA Coral Reef Watch CoralTemp dataset

Development and supporting tools

  • GitHub and Git
  • SuperCollider scripts and sound-design references
  • Visual Studio Code
